correctness.rationale: The max-metric distance in a strong product is used exactly. The bipartite auxiliary graph is reconstructed with a shortest-odd-cycle sign argument. Both independent classes of any 2m-vertex GP set must project bijectively to the unique m-leaf maximum GP set in K_{1,m} for m>=3; hence each leaf occurs twice and no star center is selected. Pair distances show there are no further geodesic obstructions involving two points in one layer; the three-layer criterion gives the complete 2/3/4-support classification. Independent choices by leaves produce the four disjoint counted terms. A BFS adjacency-level exhaustive verifier tests 1,641,522 candidate subsets over stated ranges and a separate positional-pair enumeration checks broader ranges, both agreeing exactly.

originality.rationale: The inspected first-public 2026 path-product source proves the scalar optimum and its bipartite auxiliary lemma but does not give maximum-set multiplicities or the star-specific support classification. The 2024 general-position-polynomial source counts other families and Cartesian products, not the present strong product. The 2025 variant-product article studies outer/dual/total rather than ordinary general position. Search results contain same-term but non-covering published-finding corpus claims about generalized windmills and multipartite dual sets. The new all-maximum-set classification and two-parameter exact enumerator are not implied by the scalar bound. Novelty remains literature-dependent rather than absolutely certified.

value.rationale: This solves the natural full optimum-solution census for path products with arbitrary stars of degree at least three, the first regime in which the star has a unique nontrivial maximal GP leaf set. Unlike the known scalar bound, it proves a four-layer rigidity theorem and exact support profiles. The coefficient is unexpectedly quadratic in path length, with a computable exponential star-degree coefficient; these multiplicities are needed to study the extremal coefficient of the general-position polynomial and cannot be recovered from the existing maximum-size formula.
